Positive Lagrangian ideals and distributions

A complex phase can suppress singularities without possessing a smooth real critical manifold. The right geometric object is its ideal of critical equations. This lesson constructs that ideal, explains its positivity, and proves the two-way passage between a positive oscillatory representation and a damped inverse Fourier representation.

We use the cotangent convention of the symplectic lesson:

Ω=∑j=1ndξj∧dxj,Hf=∑j(fξj∂xj−fxj∂ξj),{f,g}=Hfg.(0.1) \Omega=\sum_{j=1}^n d\xi_j\wedge dx_j,\qquad H_f=\sum_j(f_{\xi_j}\partial_{x_j}-f_{x_j}\partial_{\xi_j}),\qquad \{f,g\}=H_fg. \tag{0.1} Ω=j=1∑n​dξj​∧dxj​,Hf​=j∑​(fξj​​∂xj​​−fxj​​∂ξj​​),{f,g}=Hf​g.(0.1)

Complexification extends Ω\OmegaΩ bilinearly. Positivity of a complex plane means iΩ(V‾,V)≥0i\Omega(\overline V,V)\ge0iΩ(V,V)≥0. Our symbols are ordinary Sμ=S1,0μS^\mu=S^\mu_{1,0}Sμ=S1,0μ​: on compact spatial sets,

∣∂xα∂θβa(x,θ)∣≤Cαβ⟨θ⟩μ−∣β∣.(0.2) |\partial_x^\alpha\partial_\theta^\beta a(x,\theta)| \le C_{\alpha\beta}\langle\theta\rangle^{\mu-|\beta|}. \tag{0.2} ∣∂xα​∂θβ​a(x,θ)∣≤Cαβ​⟨θ⟩μ−∣β∣.(0.2)

All phase statements are local near a marked nonzero frequency. Amplitudes have small closed conic support inside the open phase domain; bounded frequencies contribute smooth functions. Ideals are ideals of complex-valued smooth functions, with locality under compact cutoffs. Geometric equality and congruence mean equality of these local ideals, rather than equality of real zero sets. For symbol residues, congruences also retain bounded normalized coefficient families, as constructed in Section 8. This additional uniformity is needed for damping estimates; Exercise 17 explains why ordinary smooth ideal membership alone is insufficient.

The preceding lessons supply symplectic critical-map geometry, real Gaussian normalization, homogeneous phase stabilization and positive complex planes. Section 4 of Real and complex symplectic normal forms of functions proves one-variable smooth complex division on a common neighborhood. The uniform complex nonstationary and stationary-phase contracts are identified below, with credit to Hörmander I. Support-preserving summation is proved in H6, the complete current symbol construction, and the Fourier localization proof is W1. The contour and Gaussian foundations supply the actual complex transversal, matrix square factors, oriented deformation identity and Gaussian branch. The proof map binds all these results to their exact earlier programme proofs. The arguments here prove the additional uniform graph division, flat-ideal, ideal elimination, symbol residue and representation steps.

1. Lagrangian ideals and their real zeros

For a real Lagrangian submanifold Λ⊂T∗X\Lambda\subset T^*XΛ⊂T∗X, let JΛJ_\LambdaJΛ​ be its smooth vanishing ideal. If fff vanishes on Λ\LambdaΛ, then dfdfdf annihilates TΛT\LambdaTΛ; the defining Hamilton identity places HfH_fHf​ in (TΛ)Ω=TΛ(T\Lambda)^\Omega=T\Lambda(TΛ)Ω=TΛ. Thus {f,g}\{f,g\}{f,g} vanishes on Λ\LambdaΛ whenever ggg does. Local submanifold coordinates give nnn real defining functions uju_juj​ with independent differentials. Taylor's integral formula in the normal variables writes every vanishing function as ∑bjuj\sum b_ju_j∑bj​uj​. Membership is local: a partition of unity assembles these representations, and away from the zero set one nonzero generator divides any function.

Conversely, suppose a real ideal is locally generated by nnn real functions with independent differentials, is Poisson closed, and has this locality property. Its common zero set MMM is a smooth codimension-nnn submanifold. The independent HujH_{u_j}Huj​​ span (TM)Ω(TM)^\Omega(TM)Ω. Poisson closure gives duk(Huj)=0du_k(H_{u_j})=0duk​(Huj​​)=0 on MMM, so (TM)Ω⊂TM(TM)^\Omega\subset TM(TM)Ω⊂TM. Both spaces have dimension nnn; equality makes MMM Lagrangian. The preceding real Taylor division and partition argument show that the original ideal is the entire vanishing ideal of MMM.

A complex Lagrangian ideal retains Poisson closure, cutoff locality and nnn local generators uju_juj​, but their differentials are independent over C\mathbb CC at each common real zero. A conic ideal admits homogeneous local generators. Define

If u~=Au\widetilde u=A uu=Au is another independent generating system, then du~=A dud\widetilde u=A\,dudu=Adu at a real zero. Independence makes AAA invertible there, proving that TyJT_yJTy​J is intrinsic. The Hamilton fields span its symplectic orthogonal; Poisson closure again places them in its kernel. The real set JRJ_{\mathbb R}JR​ need not be a manifold of dimension nnn. A complex equation imposes both its real and imaginary parts, while its differential condition counts complex equations. Section 11 gives an ideal whose real zeros cross and whose positive tangent rank changes along that crossing.

g(t,z)=q(t,z)f(t,z)+r(z).(2.1) g(t,z)=q(t,z)f(t,z)+r(z). \tag{2.1} g(t,z)=q(t,z)f(t,z)+r(z).(2.1)

This is smooth division by a complex equation in real variables. Its complete almost-analytic extension, complex-root and flat-error proof is in Section 4 of Real and complex symplectic normal forms of functions. It gives the multiple-equation version by induction. Reorder the real variables and equations to obtain a nonzero first pivot. At the marked zero their Jacobian is the Schur complement of the first pivot, so it is invertible. Inductively divide by those residues. 4. A homogeneous generating function in adapted coordinates

At a real zero of a conic Lagrangian ideal, choose cotangent coordinates whose horizontal plane dξ=0d\xi=0dξ=0 is transverse to TyJT_yJTy​J. Such coordinates come from a real change of base variables. To see existence, apply the common-transversal argument from the linear Lagrangian lesson over C\mathbb CC: some graph dξ=B dxd\xi=B\,dxdξ=Bdx, with BBB complex symmetric, is transverse to the given plane. Its transversality determinant is a nonzero polynomial in the symmetric entries of BBB. A polynomial vanishing for all real entries vanishes identically, so a real symmetric BBB also works. At a nonzero covector any such second-derivative adjustment is realized by a base change with identity first derivative: contract its second derivatives with the marked covector, using one nonzero component to prescribe the desired symmetric matrix. The exact base map and its full cotangent derivative are given in foundation A0, (A1); it constructs this horizontal plane with identity first derivative at the mark. That proof also verifies the complex linear argument and the real determinant-polynomial step.

12. Bundle-valued distributions and microlocal locality

Let E→XE\to XE→X be a smooth vector bundle and JJJ a positive conic Lagrangian ideal. A distribution section belongs to Im(X,J;E)I^m(X,J;E)Im(X,J;E) when, at every (x0,ξ0)∈JR(x_0,\xi_0)\in J_{\mathbb R}(x0​,ξ0​)∈JR​, a local frame for EEE and a positive phase parametrizing JJJ give a representation (7.1), component by component with amplitudes in Sm+(n−2N)/4S^{m+(n-2N)/4}Sm+(n−2N)/4, modulo a distribution smooth microlocally at that point. The requirement can equivalently use every such phase: pass from the first representation to (10.2), then apply the converse of Section 10 to any second phase. Representative changes of HHH give only smooth errors by Section 9.

A change of bundle frame multiplies the amplitude by a smooth invertible matrix, preserving its symbol order and the microlocal equality. Base-coordinate changes pull back the phase and amplitudes, preserving positivity and generator independence. Thus this definition is intrinsic. If JJJ is defined only in an open cotangent cone, impose the same condition only there; all assertions and restrictions are microlocal.

The local leading residue (10.3) is useful, but this lesson does not identify it with a complete global complex principal-symbol bundle. Gluing those residues must also track the damping factor and its infinite-order gauge. That additional structure is distinct from the real Maslov construction and is not a consequence of a tangent-plane positivity test.

13. Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (Real ideal converse). In symplectic dimension 2n2n2n, suppose nnn independent real generators are Poisson closed modulo their ideal. Prove that their real common zero set is Lagrangian and that every smooth function vanishing there belongs locally to the ideal.

Solution. Independence gives a smooth codimension-nnn zero set MMM. The Hamilton fields are independent and span (TM)Ω(TM)^\Omega(TM)Ω, because their defining covectors span the annihilator of TMTMTM. Their derivatives on every generator vanish on MMM, so they are tangent. Equal dimensions give (TM)Ω=TM(TM)^\Omega=TM(TM)Ω=TM. In coordinates (s,t)(s,t)(s,t) with the generators as ttt, a vanishing function is g(s,t)=∑jtj∫01∂tjg(s,τt)dτg(s,t)=\sum_jt_j\int_0^1\partial_{t_j}g(s,\tau t)d\taug(s,t)=∑j​tj​∫01​∂tj​​g(s,τt)dτ. This is the required ideal representation. Cutoffs and a partition of unity give the local-to-global statement on any region where the ideal has the stated locality property.

Hξξ=(z2/r3−z/r2−z/r21/r). H_{\xi\xi}=\begin{pmatrix}z^2/r^3&-z/r^2\\-z/r^2&1/r\end{pmatrix}. Hξξ​=(z2/r3−z/r2​−z/r21/r​).

Its product with (r,z)t(r,z)^t(r,z)t is zero, while rHr+zHz=2r+z2/(2r)=HrH_r+zH_z=2r+z^2/(2r)=HrHr​+zHz​=2r+z2/(2r)=H. With uj=xj−Hξju_j=x_j-H_{\xi_j}uj​=xj​−Hξj​​, (0.1) gives {uj,uk}=∂ξkHξj−∂ξjHξk=0\{u_j,u_k\}=\partial_{\xi_k}H_{\xi_j}-\partial_{\xi_j}H_{\xi_k}=0{uj​,uk​}=∂ξk​​Hξj​​−∂ξj​​Hξk​​=0. The gradient is constant on each ray, so the zero set is conic. These identities require degree one for HHH.

Exercise 3 (A residue sign check). For one graph variable T=iyT=iyT=iy, derive the sign in (2.7). Explain why a nonholomorphic extension's error cannot simply be omitted.

Solution. The chain rule along Vs=T+s(v−T)V_s=T+s(v-T)Vs​=T+s(v−T) yields (v−T)∂VA+(v−T‾)∂V‾A(v-T)\partial_VA+(v-\overline T)\partial_{\overline V}A(v−T)∂V​A+(v−T)∂V​A. Since v−T‾=(v−T)+2iyv-\overline T=(v-T)+2iyv−T=(v−T)+2iy, integrating produces E=+2iy∫01∂V‾A(Vs)dsE=+2iy\int_0^1\partial_{\overline V}A(V_s)dsE=+2iy∫01​∂V​A(Vs​)ds. A smooth almost-analytic extension has a flat, generally nonzero antiholomorphic derivative. Omitting it changes the identity. Its flatness instead permits exact division by v−Tv-Tv−T through (v−T)‾E/∣v−T∣2\overline{(v-T)}E/|v-T|^2(v−T)​E/∣v−T∣2, with smooth zero extension as proved in Section 2.

Solution. Here Hr=iz2/(2r2)H_r=iz^2/(2r^2)Hr​=iz2/(2r2), Hz=−iz/rH_z=-iz/rHz​=−iz/r. Both are real exactly when z=0z=0z=0, and then both vanish. Exercise 6 (A singular real critical set). For (11.3), describe the real zeros and compute the positive tangent rank on each branch and at the intersection.

Solution. Write G=z2w2/r3G=z^2w^2/r^3G=z2w2/r3. Its zero set is z=0z=0z=0 or w=0w=0w=0, and all its first derivatives vanish there. Thus Hξ=0H_\xi=0Hξ​=0 there and the real zeros are exactly x=0x=0x=0 over those branches. On z=0,w≠0z=0,w\ne0z=0,w=0, the only nonzero Hessian entry of GGG is Gzz=2w2/r3G_{zz}=2w^2/r^3Gzz​=2w2/r3; the positive form −2Im⁡Hξξ=2Gξξ-2\operatorname{Im}H_{\xi\xi}=2G_{\xi\xi}−2ImHξξ​=2Gξξ​ has rank one. On the other branch the nonzero entry is Gww=2z2/r3G_{ww}=2z^2/r^3Gww​=2z2/r3, again rank one. At the intersection the Hessian vanishes, so the rank is zero. The angular axes cross, proving the real zero set is singular despite independent complex graph generators.

Exercise 7 (Tangent positivity is insufficient). Prove that (11.4) gives positive tangent planes at all real zeros but cannot represent a positive ideal on a cone around z=0z=0z=0.

Solution. Its imaginary gradient is (−2z3/r3,3z2/r2)(-2z^3/r^3,3z^2/r^2)(−2z3/r3,3z2/r2), vanishing exactly at z=0z=0z=0; its Hessian also vanishes there. Therefore (5.12) is zero and is positive. On r=1r=1r=1, however, Im⁡H=z3\operatorname{Im}H=z^3ImH=z3, taking both signs. Any same-ideal representative has gradient difference bounded by arbitrary powers of the imaginary gradient, hence value difference O(∣z∣2L)O(|z|^{2L})O(∣z∣2L) by Euler. Take L=2L=2L=2: the cubic term retains its sign for small positive zzz. No nonpositive-imaginary representative exists on that cone. By Section 5 this precludes positive phase realization.

The same bound survives sufficiently small matrix perturbations.

Exercise 9 (Actual partial elimination). For (11.5), verify the phase rank condition, compute its full marked determinant, and prove (11.6) with its branch.

Solution. At x=η=0x=\eta=0x=η=0, the critical derivatives are φρ=x+iεx2/2−(1+ib)η2/(2ρ2)\varphi_\rho=x+i\varepsilon x^2/2-(1+ib)\eta^2/(2\rho^2)φρ​=x+iεx2/2−(1+ib)η2/(2ρ2) and φη=(1+ib)η/ρ\varphi_\eta=(1+ib)\eta/\rhoφη​=(1+ib)η/ρ. Φ=(iερ1010000(1+ib)/ρ),det⁡(Φ/i)=b−iρ. \Phi=\begin{pmatrix}i\varepsilon\rho&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&(1+ib)/\rho\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det(\Phi/i)=\frac{b-i}{\rho}. Φ=​iερ10​100​00(1+ib)/ρ​​,det(Φ/i)=ρb−i​.

The integral over η\etaη is the convergent Gaussian with coefficient (b−i)/(2ρ)(b-i)/(2\rho)(b−i)/(2ρ), whose real part is positive. Exercise 10 (Mellin partition and symbol order). Let ρ∈Cc∞(R)\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)ρ∈Cc∞​(R) have integral one, and r>0r>0r>0. Evaluate ∫0∞ρ(log⁡(r/t))dt/t\int_0^\infty\rho(\log(r/t))dt/t∫0∞​ρ(log(r/t))dt/t, and evaluate the same integral with factor tμt^\mutμ. Explain how this controls the order in (8.5).

Solution. Substitute s=log⁡(r/t)s=\log(r/t)s=log(r/t), so dt/t=−dsdt/t=-dsdt/t=−ds, with the endpoints reversed. The first integral is 1. The second is

rμ∫Re−μsρ(s)ds. r^\mu\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\mu s}\rho(s)ds. rμ∫R​e−μsρ(s)ds.

The moment is a finite constant. On the bump support t/rt/rt/r lies in a fixed compact positive interval, so each frequency derivative of a bounded normalized coefficient costs r−1r^{-1}r−1. Exercise 11 (Damping a flat angular amplitude). On r>0r>0r>0, let s=z/rs=z/rs=z/r, H=−iz2/(2r)H=-iz^2/(2r)H=−iz2/(2r), and v=rνe−1/s2v=r^\nu e^{-1/s^2}v=rνe−1/s2 for s≠0s\ne0s=0, extended by zero at s=0s=0s=0, with fixed angular and low-frequency cutoffs. Prove that e−iHve^{-iH}ve−iHv is rapidly decreasing with every frequency derivative on this cone.

Solution. Every angular derivative of the flat factor is bounded by CL∣s∣2LC_L|s|^{2L}CL​∣s∣2L for arbitrary LLL. Since G=rs2/2G=rs^2/2G=rs2/2, this bounds a derivative of vvv by CαLrν−∣α∣−LGLC_{\alpha L}r^{\nu-|\alpha|-L}G^LCαL​rν−∣α∣−LGL. Multiplication by e−Ge^{-G}e−G makes GLe−GG^Le^{-G}GLe−G bounded. Exponential derivatives contain bounded first derivatives of HHH and decreasing higher derivatives. For any desired decay and fixed derivative order, choose LLL larger than their finite order cost plus ν\nuν. This proves the assertion. Exercise 12 (All constants and orders). Verify (10.5), (10.7) and (10.8). If one parameter is removed by a Gaussian integration, prove that the distribution order mmm stays unchanged.

Solution. The exponent of 2π2\pi2π is −(n+2N)/4+(n+N)/2=n/4-(n+2N)/4+(n+N)/2=n/4−(n+2N)/4+(n+N)/2=n/4. Also μ+(N−n)/2−j=m−n/4−j=σ−j\mu+(N-n)/2-j=m-n/4-j=\sigma-jμ+(N−n)/2−j=m−n/4−j=σ−j, and μ+N−(n+N)/2−L=σ−L\mu+N-(n+N)/2-L=\sigma-Lμ+N−(n+N)/2−L=σ−L. When NNN becomes N−1N-1N−1, the amplitude order required by (10.1) becomes μ+1/2\mu+1/2μ+1/2, exactly the Gaussian determinant order for the removed parameter. The prefactor in (7.1) becomes (2π)1/2(2\pi)^{1/2}(2π)1/2 times its old value, exactly the Gaussian constant. Thus both orders and constants give the same mmm.

Exercise 13 (Why an absolute error cannot be undamped). Suppose G(ξ)=c∣ξ∣G(\xi)=c|\xi|G(ξ)=c∣ξ∣, c>0c>0c>0, and EL(ξ)=O(∣ξ∣−L)E_L(\xi)=O(|\xi|^{-L})EL​(ξ)=O(∣ξ∣−L) for every LLL. Does this imply eGELe^{G}E_LeGEL​ is a symbol? Give a single smooth counterexample and explain why (10.9) still follows.

Solution. With a smooth cutoff near zero, take E(ξ)=e−∣ξ∣E(\xi)=e^{-\sqrt{|\xi|}}E(ξ)=e−∣ξ∣​ for ∣ξ∣≥1|\xi|\ge1∣ξ∣≥1. It and all its derivatives decay faster than every power, but ec∣ξ∣Ee^{c|\xi|}Eec∣ξ∣E grows faster than every power and is not a symbol of any finite order. In (10.9) the summed symbol tail is multiplied by e−Ge^{-G}e−G, whose modulus is at most one. We therefore compare the Fourier transform directly with this damped tail and the absolute stationary-phase error, obtaining arbitrary decay without multiplying an error by eGe^GeG.

Exercise 14 (Converse correction with support). Explain why the reverse construction of Section 10 can correct every lower symbol order on the same cone. Why is an amplitude-dependent sequence of shrinking cones insufficient?

Solution. The phase graph, its invertible generator blocks and the normalized annular cutoffs determine one division patch before amplitudes are chosen. Section 2 constructs bounded-family divisions there; the constants and almost-analytic radii may change, but the patch does not. Hence (10.10) gives aj∈Sμ−ja_j\in S^{\mu-j}aj​∈Sμ−j with the same fixed support for each residual Rj∈Sσ−jR_j\in S^{\sigma-j}Rj​∈Sσ−j. Support-preserving summation produces a single amplitude having all these asymptotic terms. The forward estimate applied to each tail yields arbitrary Fourier decay on that same cone. If the cones shrank with jjj, there need not be any open cone on which all orders hold, so the required microlocal smoothness would not follow.

Exercise 15 (Some phase and every phase). Prove independence of the phase and the bundle frame in the definition of Im(X,J;E)I^m(X,J;E)Im(X,J;E).

Solution. Represent in one local frame using a phase φ\varphiφ. The forward theorem gives a normal frequency symbol of order m−n/4m-n/4m−n/4. Another positive phase ψ\psiψ for the same ideal has the same normal graph ideal; any choice of its HHH differs by the all-power ambiguity in Section 4, which changes the damped distribution only smoothly by Section 9. The converse for ψ\psiψ now gives a representation with amplitude order m+(n−2Nψ)/4m+(n-2N_\psi)/4m+(n−2Nψ​)/4. Multiplication by the smooth frame-change matrix preserves ordinary symbol bounds and multiplies the microlocally smooth difference by a smooth matrix. Thus both choices preserve the definition, component by component.

Exercise 16 (Wavefront containment can be strict). Give a positive nondegenerate phase with a nonempty real critical image and an amplitude whose distribution is smooth. Explain which estimate proves smoothness.

Solution. Use φ=x⋅θ\varphi=x\cdot\thetaφ=x⋅θ near any nonzero θ0\theta_0θ0​. Its critical equations are x=0x=0x=0 with independent differentials, and its critical image contains (0,θ0)(0,\theta_0)(0,θ0​). Choose a smooth amplitude compactly supported in both xxx and a bounded frequency annulus inside that cone. The integral and every xxx derivative converge absolutely, since the frequency support is compact. It is therefore smooth, with empty wavefront set, even though the phase's critical image is nonempty. Equivalently, integration of its localized Fourier transform gives arbitrary decay. This verifies why (7.6) is an inclusion rather than an equality.

14. Source and dependency notes

The geometric and representation results correspond to Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators IV, §25.4, printed pages 35–43: Definition 25.4.1, Proposition 25.4.2, Definition 25.4.3, Proposition 25.4.4, Corollary 25.4.5, Definition 25.4.6, Theorem 25.4.7, Lemma 25.4.8 and Definition 25.4.9. The whole section, including the representation converse, is used. The source statement's degree discrepancy is identified in Section 4.

The division input and its induction are located in Hörmander I, Theorems 7.5.6–7.5.9; flat-residue source context is Lemmas 7.5.10–7.5.11 and Theorem 7.5.12, pages 203–204. Complex nonstationary phase is Theorem 7.7.1, pages 216–218. Critical-value and uniform complex stationary-phase context is Lemmas 7.7.8–7.7.9, Theorem 7.7.12 and Proposition 7.7.13, pages 224–228. Positive oscillatory extension and wavefront context are Theorem 7.8.2, pages 236–238, and Theorem 8.1.9, pages 260–261. We supply the ordinary-symbol dyadic proofs needed here; broader symbol classes require their own estimates.
